episodes.title: Three doors, one index
episodes.subtitle: The same words can support very different admission rules.

scenes.title: The result is missing banana
narration: You search for apple, orange, banana. A result appears that contains apple and orange, but no banana. Has the engine stopped searching for words? Has it understood some deeper meaning? Make a prediction before looking behind the search box.
A perfectly ordinary lexical system can do this. The crucial question is which analysed terms were compulsory. Matching words and requiring every word are different decisions.

scenes.title: Four records. Keep the evidence fixed.
narration: Keep the chapter's tiny collection fixed. A contains apple, orange and banana. B contains apple and orange. C contains apple. D contains pear and grape. These cards show term presence, not repetition counts or complete document lengths.
Nothing about the vocabulary or the index has changed. Now turn just one control: how many of the three query terms must a record match to become eligible?

scenes.title: Change only the admission rule
narration: Require all three terms, and only A gets in. Require at least two, and A and B get in. Let any one term suffice, and A, B and C get in. D has no query terms and stays out.
Every arrangement still uses lexical evidence. The any-match eligible set is the union of the posting lists, expressible as Boolean OR. A separate scoring rule can supply graded rankings.

scenes.title: Eligibility does not determine order
narration: Keep any-match admission. A, B and C may compete. Suppose a scoring rule orders them B, A, C. This order is stipulated, exactly as in the chapter. These cards do not contain enough information to calculate BM twenty-five scores.
Matching more distinct terms does not guarantee a higher BM twenty-five score. Term rarity, frequency and document length also matter. Three matches do not automatically beat two.

scenes.title: C qualified. C still disappears.
narration: Now retain only the first two records. B and A are returned. C qualified, but fell below the output boundary. D never qualified. Both are absent from the final pair, for completely different reasons.
Admission asks who may compete. Ranking asks how the candidates are ordered. A top k boundary asks how many leaders are retained. Changing one control need not change the other two.

scenes.title: A count is not a window into the engine
narration: The chapter's Google Scholar example separates another three things: the reported match count, relevance ordering, and the set a person can actually view. Its supplied example reports about nine point four million matches, while help documents a one thousand result display limit.

That limit is an observable presentation boundary. It does not reveal every scoring signal, whether every match received a final score, or whether the displayed set is a global top k. We are reading the chapter's evidence, not testing today's service.

scenes.title: What did the missing word establish?
narration: Return to the missing banana. A result lacking a typed word can be consistent with lexical retrieval. It does not identify the complete architecture behind the interface. Even the apparent absence of a match may need closer inspection.

Before naming the engine, separate the controls. What terms reached retrieval? Which conditions were required? How were candidates scored? And what output could you see? The next investigation changes a query term while keeping those questions separate.

episodes.title: One bad word, two failures
episodes.subtitle: A weak expansion can exclude a useful record—or distort its competition.

scenes.title: One more word. Better search?
narration: Start with delulu, job, interview, expectations. Someone adds foolish as a supposed alternative for delulu. Does adding this word make the search safer because the original terms are still there? Try to predict what happens under two different admission rules.

The same weak term can cause two different kinds of damage. A compulsory term can exclude a record. An optional scoring term can shift the competition. Neither result requires the engine to malfunction.

scenes.title: Two records from the Evidence Lab
narration: Meet two records from the chapter's BM twenty-five Evidence Lab. Record A is Delulu expectations during a job interview. It contains all four original query terms and no foolish. Record F is Why foolish job applicants misread the interview.

F contains foolish, job and interview, but lacks delulu and expectations. These are teaching records from a six-record collection. Their usefulness still depends on the searcher's need; term matches alone do not settle that judgment.

scenes.title: All five required: both records fail
narration: Under implied AND, all five terms are compulsory. A passed the original four conditions. Adding foolish now excludes it before ranking begins. F fails too, because it lacks delulu and expectations.
Imagine A is exactly what you needed. A better ranker cannot recover it from this candidate set: A never arrived. You would need to change the retrieval conditions or run another retrieval pass.

scenes.title: Any match: the extra evidence stays
narration: Switch to any-match BM twenty-five. A remains eligible through its original matches. F also remains eligible through its matches. Adding foolish gives F an additional matching term that contributes to its score.
A has not been excluded, but its competition can change. We are not asserting a numerical order for A and F here. Admission and scoring influence are enough to explain the two different risks.

scenes.title: Rare does not mean a good synonym
narration: In the lab's six-record collection, only F contains foolish. A rare term can receive high inverse document frequency, giving its matches extra weight. But rarity answers a collection question: how widely does this term occur?
It does not answer the searcher's question: is this a good way to express my need? A statistical weight cannot turn a weak substitute into a good concept. More weight can amplify a poor choice.

scenes.title: Saturation cannot repair the concept
narration: Could term-frequency saturation fix it? Saturation limits the extra benefit of repeating the same term inside a document. That is useful when twenty mentions should not get twenty times the credit. It is a different problem.

Saturation does not inspect whether foolish represents the intended concept. A weak query term can still contribute lexical evidence. Neither a smooth score nor a sophisticated ranking formula guarantees a well-formed query.

scenes.title: Check the term, then check its job
narration: Compare the search with and without the weak term. Inspect which records enter, which disappear, and which gain scoring evidence. Keep the collection and other settings fixed so the comparison has a clear interpretation.

Then ask what job the extra term is doing. Is it compulsory, one alternative in a group, or optional scoring evidence? The engine can execute your instructions correctly while those instructions express the wrong need. Inspect the proposed expansion before trusting it.

episodes.title: Four lives of a missing word
episodes.subtitle: One visible absence, several possible histories.

scenes.title: The title has no delulu. What happened?
narration: You type delulu, job, interview. A result title says only Job interview expectations. Where did delulu go? It is tempting to tell a story about a clever semantic engine. But the same screen can fit several very different histories.
Follow four possible routes. Each is a mechanism the chapter asks us to check, not a diagnosis of a named product. Several routes could operate in the same search.

scenes.title: History 1: removed during analysis
narration: First, a word can disappear during routine analysis. In the chapter's illustration, you type the job interview. An optional stop-word rule removes the. Retrieval receives job interview. The discarded word was never a condition at lookup.

This example depends on the analyser. It does not say every system removes the same words. Tokenisation, normalisation, stemming and stop-word handling prepare strings for matching; none by itself establishes understanding of meaning.

scenes.title: History 2: changed during rewriting
narration: Second, an upstream rewrite can change what retrieval receives. You type delulu job expectations. A transformation replaces delulu with unrealistic. Retrieval then looks for unrealistic job expectations. The original word need not appear in a matching record.

Unlike routine analysis, this is an explicit reformulation. The illustration is not evidence that a particular product made this rewrite. To establish that, inspect the processed query or obtain documentation about that stage.

scenes.title: History 3: it survived, but was optional
narration: Third, delulu can remain in the retrieval input without being required. An any-match rule admits a record containing job and interview. A delulu match could add scoring evidence, but its absence need not exclude the record.

An optional term might even have no posting list anywhere in the index. Other terms can still admit records. Make that unmatched term compulsory under strict AND, and the eligible set is empty. The difference is the execution rule.

scenes.title: History 4: the match is out of view
narration: Fourth, the term may have matched evidence you cannot see in the excerpt. The visible title says Job interview expectations. The indexed abstract says, We examine delulu expectations. A lexical match occurred, but the title did not display it.

Other indexed fields, expanded terms, older indexed versions or off-page evidence may also matter. Inspect the searchable fields and the indexed representation before concluding that no lexical match happened. A snippet is only a small window.

scenes.title: Four jobs between keyboard and index
narration: Keep four jobs distinct. Analysis prepares strings. Execution rules decide which clauses are required, optional or subject to a minimum match. Query understanding interprets things such as entities, dates, phrases or intent. Transformation changes what retrieval receives.

Understanding can inform a decision while leaving every word unchanged. It becomes relevant to a missing word when its interpretation causes a change. Understanding alone is not a fifth history that magically removes a term.

scenes.title: A natural-language door can lead to lexical search
narration: A question in natural language can pass through a parser or language model that constructs a Boolean expression. The lexical engine can then apply Boolean admission and BM twenty-five ranking over an inverted index.

The form of the input does not identify the retrieval method. To bridge a vocabulary gap, one route changes the query and keeps lexical matching. Another changes the representation so related texts can be retrieved without shared analysed terms.

scenes.title: The screen leaves the mechanism open
narration: Return to the title without delulu. Was the word removed in analysis, changed in a rewrite, retained as optional, or matched outside the excerpt? The title alone cannot choose among them. A product name and a result count cannot settle it either.

Ask for the processed query, the admission rules, the indexed fields and evidence about the retrieval pipeline. Part One separates lexical search from strict all-term Boolean search. The next chapters investigate representations, while keeping the rest of the pipeline in view.
